arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:151108.texto: A distinctive landscape painter of the 19th century, George Inness excelled at capturing the poetics and mood of his environs, finding spiritual resonances in nature, from its grand vistas to its quiet nooks. The Mill Pond depicts a sylvan setting, in which a small figure rows a boat in the pond at middle distance. Brilliant pigments of orange, green, and blue electrify an otherwise tranquil scene. Through color and atmosphere rather than line or detail, Inness communicated an intensity of vision, fueled by an individual encounter with nature.
aic:151108.title: The Mill Pond

aic:4758.texto:
“What say you to a summer morning?” John Constable wrote of this painting in a letter to a friend. Even after many years living in London, Constable continued to portray the countryside, dear to him from boyhood. Stoke-by-Nayland lies a few miles from his native village of East Bergholt in Suffolk. In this view, he divided the canvas between a brilliant, airy vista toward the hamlet on the left and a shady, tunnel-like country lane leading off to the right. Constable explained in his letter that the painting depicted a speciﬁc time, a morning in “July or August, at eight or nine o’clock, after a slight shower during the night, to enhance the dews in the shadowed part of the picture.” The artist emphasized the abundance of water through his painting technique, ﬂecking the surface with white highlights to create an effect of sparkling wetness. Here, the whole scene appears dewy, with a stream and puddles in the foreground and a central tree that droops from the weight of rainwater, emphasizing the fertile land.
Painted as much with a palette knife as with brushes, Stoke-by-Nayland lacks the ﬁnish of pictures Constable exhibited publicly; it was meant as a full-scale sketch for a work that he never realized. Nonetheless, this canvas seems to capture Constable’s delight in freely scribbling and scraping the image into existence—what it lacks in detail it gains in atmosphere. The roughness of the surface evokes the textures of real landscape, and the coexistence of natural and built elements in the scene embodies an ideal of harmony indicative of Constable’s vision of rural England.
aic:4758.title: Stoke-by-Nayland

aic:97292.texto: Robert Vonnoh was among the first American painters to explore Impressionism. He received his formative artistic training in Boston and headed to Paris in the early 1880s for further instruction. By the late 1880s, Vonnoh had settled in Grez-sur-Loing, a rural area outside of Paris that attracted a growing colony of artists who worked outdoors. Here, using a brilliant palette, broken brushstrokes, and unblended colors, Vonnoh captured the budding vegetation and warming sunlight of a spring day. Intense greens, peaches, and lavenders convey the dappled light and shadows of a winding road at right. The fence posts marking the edge of the yard and white linens hanging from a nearby tree highlight the scene’s domestic setting.
aic:97292.title: Spring in France

cma:148968.texto: With its beautifully rendered trees, grassy slopes, and water bathed in late afternoon sunlight, this painting clearly suggests Nanteuil's love of nature. In 1837 he wrote to a friend: "I often spend several hours . . . looking at beautiful plants with large leaves, cut out like sumptuous lace, tall grasses in ponds, their color silky and the beautiful reflections they make in the water, the little flowers with thousands of colours the ground is embroidered with, all provide me with a source of enjoyment." Although the forest Nanteuil described seems very real, his painting includes a satyr. Seated on a stone near a stream, the half human, half goat mythological figure seems lost in the music he plays upon his pipes. Nanteuil is most famous for his lithographs and etchings; paintings by the artist are rather rare.
cma:148968.title: In the Forest

cma:150054.texto: This view of a rocky landscape along the Mediterranean coast of southern France reflects the naturalist ambition of capturing exact details and atmospheric effects observed directly from life. Clear, intense light floods over the stony cliffs and the sparse greenery baked in the heat of sun. The artist, l Guigou, studied art in Marseilles and devoted most of his career to painting views of his native Provence. In 1855 he began traveling back and forth between Marseilles and Paris, where he became familiar with the paintings of Gustave Courbet and died of a stroke at age 37.
cma:150054.title: Landscape at Saint-André, Near Marseilles

cma:150054.texto: Guigou was once the drawing master for the children of Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild.

afirmaciones.texto: La obra refleja la ambición naturalista de capturar detalles exactos y efectos atmosféricos observados directamente de la vida, con luz clara e intensa que inunda los acantilados rocosos y la vegetación escasa bajo el calor del sol.
La escena muestra un paisaje rocoso y seco con poca vegetación, lo que da una sensación más estática y menos vibrante.

El artista capturó la vegetación que brota y la luz cálida de un día de primavera usando una paleta brillante, pinceladas rotas y colores no mezclados, transmitiendo la luz moteada y las sombras de un camino serpenteante.
Los colores intensos y la representación de la luz y sombra dan una sensación de vida y movimiento en la escena.
La pintura representa una mañana de verano después de una ligera lluvia, con efectos de rocío y humedad resaltados por la técnica del artista, que crea un efecto de brillo y frescura en el paisaje.
La escena tiene una atmósfera fresca y húmeda, con un paisaje que parece vivo por la presencia del agua y la luz que refleja en ella.
La pintura muestra árboles, pendientes cubiertas de hierba y agua bañada por la luz del atardecer, reflejando el amor del artista por la naturaleza y la belleza de las plantas y flores.
La inclusión de un sátiro mitológico tocando la flauta añade un elemento de fantasía y vida a la escena natural.
La escena transmite una sensación de serenidad y vida a través de la representación detallada y luminosa de la naturaleza y la figura mitológica.
El artista capturó la poética y el estado de ánimo del entorno natural, mostrando un paisaje con un pequeño bote y un remero en el estanque, usando pigmentos brillantes para electrificar la escena.
El uso de colores brillantes y la atmósfera transmiten una intensidad de visión y una sensación de vida en la naturaleza, a pesar de la tranquilidad de la escena.

plan.nota_de_identidad: Clase **1 / 2** (la tabla de identidades), el **híbrido**: se *direcciona* como caché de entradas —eso **es** el reuso del plan al barrer el peso de fusión, cinco corridas de un barrido de `α` reusando un plan— y su contenido es la salida **no determinista** de un LLM. Por eso la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica y lo que rige es **escritura única** (la escritura única del plan). lo que no entra en la identidad del plan: `α`, N, la fusión y el `variante_id` **no** son ingredientes. la versión del prompt como ingrediente del plan: el prompt **+ su versión**, el modelo y el muestreo **sí**.
plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.
plan.nota_de_pl5: la escritura única del plan: un `plan_id` se escribe **una sola vez**; si ya existe se **lee** y la corrida registra si lo **produjo o lo reusó**. Sin ese registro no habría forma de saber **qué corrida pagó la llamada que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura cuenta**.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

   La obra refleja la ambición naturalista de capturar detalles exactos y efectos atmosféricos observados directamente de la vida, con luz clara e intensa que inunda los acantilados rocosos y la vegetación escasa bajo el calor del sol. [1]
   La escena muestra un paisaje rocoso y seco con poca vegetación, lo que da una sensación más estática y menos vibrante.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This view of a rocky landscape along the Mediterranean coast of southern France reflects the naturalist ambition of capturing exact details and atmospheric effects observed directly from life. Clear, intense light floods over the stony cliffs and the sparse greenery baked in the heat of sun. The artist, l Guigou, studied art in Marseilles and devoted most of his career to painting views of his native Provence. In 1855 he began traveling back and forth between Marseilles and Paris, where he became familiar with the paintings of Gustave Courbet and died of a stroke at age 37.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1980.265 · CC0 1.0

2. **Spring in France**
   Robert William Vonnoh · 1890 · Oil on canvas · Impressionism
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/97292

   El artista capturó la vegetación que brota y la luz cálida de un día de primavera usando una paleta brillante, pinceladas rotas y colores no mezclados, transmitiendo la luz moteada y las sombras de un camino serpenteante. [1]
   Los colores intensos y la representación de la luz y sombra dan una sensación de vida y movimiento en la escena.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Robert Vonnoh was among the first American painters to explore Impressionism. He received his formative artistic training in Boston and headed to Paris in the early 1880s for further instruction. By the late 1880s, Vonnoh had settled in Grez-sur-Loing, a rural area outside of Paris that attracted a growing colony of artists who worked outdoors. Here, using a brilliant palette, broken brushstrokes, and unblended colors, Vonnoh captured the budding vegetation and warming sunlight of a spring day. Intense greens, peaches, and lavenders convey the dappled light and shadows of a winding road at right. The fence posts marking the edge of the yard and white linens hanging from a nearby tree highlight the scene’s domestic setting.”

3. **Stoke-by-Nayland**
   John Constable · 1836 · Oil on canvas · 19th century
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758

   La pintura representa una mañana de verano después de una ligera lluvia, con efectos de rocío y humedad resaltados por la técnica del artista, que crea un efecto de brillo y frescura en el paisaje. [1]
   La escena tiene una atmósfera fresca y húmeda, con un paisaje que parece vivo por la presencia del agua y la luz que refleja en ella.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] ““What say you to a summer morning?” John Constable wrote of this painting in a letter to a friend. Even after many years living in London, Constable continued to portray the countryside, dear to him from boyhood. Stoke-by-Nayland lies a few miles from his native village of East Bergholt in Suffolk. In this view, he divided the canvas between a brilliant, airy vista toward the hamlet on the left and a shady, tunnel-like country lane leading off to the right. Constable explained in his letter that the painting depicted a speciﬁc time, a morning in “July or August, at eight or nine o’clock, after a slight shower during the night, to enhance the dews in the shadowed part of the picture.” The artist emphasized the abundance of water through his painting technique, ﬂecking the surface with white highlights to create an effect of sparkling wetness. Here, the whole scene appears dewy, with a stream and puddles in the foreground and a central tree that droops from the weight of rainwater, emphasizing the fertile land.
Painted as much with a palette knife as with brushes, Stoke-by-Nayland lacks the ﬁnish of pictures Constable exhibited publicly; it was meant as a full-scale sketch for a work that he never realized. Nonetheless, this canvas seems to capture Constable’s delight in freely scribbling and scraping the image into existence—what it lacks in detail it gains in atmosphere. The roughness of the surface evokes the textures of real landscape, and the coexistence of natural and built elements in the scene embodies an ideal of harmony indicative of Constable’s vision of rural England.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758 · CC BY 4.0
       “Stoke-by-Nayland”, John Constable. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/4758

4. **In the Forest**
   Célestin François Nanteuil · 1841 · oil on fabric
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1977.125

   La pintura muestra árboles, pendientes cubiertas de hierba y agua bañada por la luz del atardecer, reflejando el amor del artista por la naturaleza y la belleza de las plantas y flores. [1]
   La inclusión de un sátiro mitológico tocando la flauta añade un elemento de fantasía y vida a la escena natural. [1]
   La escena transmite una sensación de serenidad y vida a través de la representación detallada y luminosa de la naturaleza y la figura mitológica.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “With its beautifully rendered trees, grassy slopes, and water bathed in late afternoon sunlight, this painting clearly suggests Nanteuil's love of nature. In 1837 he wrote to a friend: "I often spend several hours . . . looking at beautiful plants with large leaves, cut out like sumptuous lace, tall grasses in ponds, their color silky and the beautiful reflections they make in the water, the little flowers with thousands of colours the ground is embroidered with, all provide me with a source of enjoyment." Although the forest Nanteuil described seems very real, his painting includes a satyr. Seated on a stone near a stream, the half human, half goat mythological figure seems lost in the music he plays upon his pipes. Nanteuil is most famous for his lithographs and etchings; paintings by the artist are rather rare.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1977.125 · CC0 1.0

   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/151108

   El artista capturó la poética y el estado de ánimo del entorno natural, mostrando un paisaje con un pequeño bote y un remero en el estanque, usando pigmentos brillantes para electrificar la escena. [1]
   El uso de colores brillantes y la atmósfera transmiten una intensidad de visión y una sensación de vida en la naturaleza, a pesar de la tranquilidad de la escena.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “A distinctive landscape painter of the 19th century, George Inness excelled at capturing the poetics and mood of his environs, finding spiritual resonances in nature, from its grand vistas to its quiet nooks. The Mill Pond depicts a sylvan setting, in which a small figure rows a boat in the pond at middle distance. Brilliant pigments of orange, green, and blue electrify an otherwise tranquil scene. Through color and atmosphere rather than line or detail, Inness communicated an intensity of vision, fueled by an individual encounter with nature.”
